title: VideoJudge: Bootstrapping Enables Scalable Supervision of MLLM-as-a-Judge for Video Understanding
claim: A generator and evaluator loop filters rating-conditioned responses into a bootstrapped dataset that fine-tunes a compact judge model.
layout: Multi-row flow, left-to-right then right-to-left, dashed feedback loop with accept/reject marks
description: A flow diagram in two rows. The top row runs left to right. A table with a rating N and gold response feeds a Generator, shown as a logo icon, guided by a blue Generation Prompt arrow. The Generator outputs a table of responses for ratings N-1 down to 1. This table goes to an Evaluator, guided by a green Evaluation Prompt arrow. The Evaluator outputs a second table of ratings and responses. A formula checks whether the mean absolute difference between generator and evaluator ratings is under a threshold. A red X sends rejected samples back along a dashed arrow to the generation prompt. A green check sends accepted samples to a stacked purple Bootstrapped Data box. The bottom row runs right to left. Bootstrapped Data goes to a pink input/output format bubble, then to a brain-chip icon labeled Small Evaluator Model by a finetune arrow. An evaluate arrow leads to a checklist icon labeled Video Understanding Eval Task Suite.
caption: Overview of our bootstrapping framework for training scalable video evaluators. A generator first produces candidate responses for a 1 to N −1 rating scale (N = 5) for each video–instruction pair. These responses are then scored by an evaluator, and only candidates whose ratings align with expectations are retained. Through an iterative refinement loop, mismatched responses are revised until they satisfy the acceptance criterion. The resulting bootstrapped dataset provides high-quality supervision signals, which we use to fine-tune compact VideoJudge models.
abstract: Precisely evaluating video understanding models remains challenging: commonly used metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore fail to capture the fineness of human judgment, while obtaining such judgments through manual evaluation is costly. Recent work has explored using large language models (LLMs) or multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) as evaluators, but their extension to video understanding remains relatively unexplored. In this work, we introduce VideoJudge, a 3B and 7B-sized MLLM judge specialized to evaluate outputs from video understanding models (\textit{i.e.}, text responses conditioned on videos). To train VideoJudge, our recipe builds on the interplay between a generator and an evaluator: the generator is prompted to produce responses conditioned on a target rating, and responses not matching the evaluator's rating are discarded. Across three out of four meta-evaluation benchmarks, VideoJudge-7B outperforms larger MLLM judge baselines such as Qwen2.5-VL (32B and 72B). Notably, we find that LLM judges (Qwen3) models perform worse than MLLM judges (Qwen2.5-VL) and long chain-of-thought reasoning does not improve performance, indicating that providing video inputs is crucial for evaluation of video understanding tasks.
